newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Jpn bank chief sees more foreign tie-ups.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Jpn bank chief sees more foreign tie-ups.

text.p: Japan's local banks will increasingly join hands with foreign banks in business alliances as "Big Bang" reforms force the sector to spruce up financial services, says the head of a Japanese banking body.

Kazumaro Kato, chairman of the Second Association of Regional Banks, predicted a growing number of such unions which will marry the strong local presence of Japan's regional banks with the innovation skills of foreign banks.

Foreign banks with experience in luring customers through attractive investment products are looking for partners to expand in Japanese markets, while regional banks want to shore up their customer base by tapping into foreign banks' expertise, he said in an interview this week with Reuters.
"Regional banks which enjoy big market share in regional markets must be attractive for foreign banks," he said.

Kato's comments followed an announcement on Monday that Japan's troubled Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd and Britain's Barclays Bank will discuss cooperation in several areas, including the development of new financial products and the securitisation of Hokkaido Takushoku's assets.

This is the second major alliance unveiled by a troubled Japanese bank and a foreign bank this year, after Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB) and Bankers Trust New York Corp announced plans for a business tie-up.
Kato said that Barclays was likely interested in individual assets in Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost main island, where Hokkaido Takushoku has maintained a strong branch network.
"As a part of Big Bang reforms, banks will be able to sell investment trust funds, and Barclays may be eager to expand such business through the tie-up," he said.

Last week Japan unveiled a blueprint for "Big Bang" reforms to break down barriers between banks, brokers and insurers, and to boost competition. The plan, aiming to lure back business which has left Japan for less regulated pastures, will force a major shake-out in Japan's financial sector, analysts say.

"(Regional) bankers are concerned that customers may change the bank they deal with if banks are slow to meet (deregulation)," said Kato, who is also president of Bank of Nagoya Ltd, based in Nagoya, central Japan.
However, he said not all regional banks are keen to form alliances with foreign banks, and the creation of such links will depend on the requirements of customers in their regions.
As the deregulation proceeds, second-tier regional banks must improve their asset quality by disposing of problem loans quickly and strengthening their capital base, he said.
Analysts have predicted some second-tier regional banks whose asset size is small will struggle to stay afloat, plagued by poor asset quality and the pressure of financial deregulation.

Japan experienced its first bank failure in five decades in 1995 when Hyogo Bank collapsed under the weight of bad loans after the bursting of Japan's asset "bubble" in the early 1990s. Two other banks, Taiheiyo and Hanwa, have also gone to the wall in the past two years. The three failed banks were all second-tier regional banks.
The Second Association of Regional Banks has 65 members, which are referred to as second-tier regional banks.

Kato said that he cannot rule out the possibility of more bank failures in the future as deregulation begins to bite. "The implementation of Big Bang reforms indicates that the possibility of bank failures will increase," he said.
He said that mergers and financial holding companies are also options for second-tier regional banks to streamline operations.
"It is also possible that the Second Association of Regional Banks will set up a (nationwide) holding firm to be joined by member banks," he said.
